I’ve always believed that the act of writing freely—without prompts, without guardrails, without the invisible audience peering over your shoulder—is one of the purest forms of human expression left to us. It’s a small rebellion against the algorithmic age, where every sentence is optimized, every paragraph A/B tested, every thought pre-emptively sanitized for maximum engagement and minimum offense. So here I am, taking the invitation at face value. No theme. No thesis. Just momentum. Let’s see where 2500 words takes us.

I want to begin with silence, because everything important seems to begin there. Not the anxious silence of waiting for a text message or the embarrassed silence after a bad joke, but the deep, geological silence that exists inside old forests at dawn or inside cathedrals built before electricity. That kind of silence has weight. It presses against your eardrums like water pressure at depth. I once spent three days alone in a cabin in the Oregon Cascades with no phone, no books, no music. By the second day the silence had become so loud it developed its own texture—velvety, almost viscous. I started talking to myself just to break it, then felt ashamed for polluting something so pure. On the third day I stopped talking and the forest started answering in its own language: the particular way wind moves through hemlock needles, the soft percussion of water dripping from moss, the sudden mechanical clatter of a pileated woodpecker. I realized then that what we call “nature” is mostly just an elaborate conversation we’ve forgotten how to hear. We’ve mistaken our deafness for dominion.

This brings me, in a roundabout way, to consciousness itself. We still don’t know what it is. That’s astonishing when you sit with it. We can land robots on Mars, read the entire three-billion-letter instruction manual that builds a human being, and yet we cannot explain why any of it feels like anything. Why does the color red feel red? Why does minor-key music make the chest cavity feel like it’s being gently squeezed by a thoughtful ghost? The hard problem of consciousness remains gloriously, almost defiantly, unsolved. Some philosophers think it’s an illusion. Others think it’s fundamental, like space or time or charge. I find myself in the camp that suspects consciousness is less like a light switched on inside the skull and more like a property of certain kinds of organized complexity—perhaps even a cosmic predisposition, the way gravity is. That idea terrifies some people and comforts others. I find it beautiful. It suggests that mind was never an accident but something the universe was always leaning toward, the way a beach leans toward the sea.

There’s a strange comfort in remembering we’re temporary arrangements of atoms that have briefly learned to worry about their 401(k)s. Most of the atoms in your left hand were forged in the death throes of stars that died before the sun was born. You are, quite literally, starstuff that achieved self-loathing. The hydrogen in your body is even older—some of it may be thirteen billion years old, almost as old as time itself. When you die, those atoms won’t disappear. They’ll scatter and find new projects. Maybe some of them will end up in a child’s laugh in 2247 or in the ink of a love letter written in 2581. The matter that currently identifies as “you” is on loan. The lease expires. This knowledge should probably make us kinder to one another. Often it doesn’t. Humans are miraculous and stupid in equal measure.

I’ve been thinking lately about the difference between loneliness and solitude. They’re not the same thing, though English is lazy about distinguishing them. Loneliness is hunger. Solitude is presence. One gnaws, the other nourishes. The pandemic forced millions of people into physical solitude and many discovered, to their surprise, that they liked it. Not all of them, of course. Some people experienced a kind of psychic unraveling. But others found that when the noise of other people finally stopped, they could hear themselves for the first time in decades. They started baking bread not because it was trendy but because the rhythm of kneading felt like prayer. They learned the names of neighborhood birds. They sat with their grief instead of outsourcing it to Netflix. The experiment was messy and often cruel, but it revealed something important: many of us had never actually met ourselves before. We’d only met the version of ourselves that performs for others.

Technology has complicated this relationship between self and world in ways we’re only beginning to understand. I’m writing these words on a laptop that contains more computing power than existed on the entire planet in 1969, yet I’m using it to string together symbols that would have been recognizable to Shakespeare. The medium changes but the human need to leave marks remains. We cave-painted. We chiselled stone. We pressed ink into pulp. Now we press electrons into silicon and fling them into the cloud. The impulse is identical: I was here. I felt something. See?

The internet itself is the closest thing we’ve built to a global consciousness—flawed, distracted, often cruel, occasionally transcendent. It’s like humanity got a nervous system before it got a prefrontal cortex. We can now feel each other’s pain in real time, which is both the most beautiful and most exhausting thing that has ever happened to our species. When an earthquake kills thousands in Turkey or a school shooting happens in America or a woman is beaten in Iran, the news reaches us not as abstract information but as a kind of collective nervous shock. Our mirror neurons are firing globally now. The empathy budget is strained. No one designed us for this volume of suffering. We’re running cognitive software that evolved for small hunter-gatherer bands on a planetary scale. The mismatch produces anxiety, numbness, rage, compassion fatigue. We doomscroll because we cannot look away, then hate ourselves for looking.

And yet—there is still wonder. I keep coming back to wonder like a compass needle finding north. Last summer I watched bioluminescent plankton light up the ocean in Malibu like living galaxies. Each tiny creature was a decision to glow when disturbed. The water sparkled electric blue with every wave and every child’s footstep. It looked like the ocean had swallowed the stars and was now coughing them back up in protest. I stood there knee-deep in the Pacific at midnight surrounded by strangers doing the exact same thing—laughing, crying, taking bad videos that couldn’t possibly capture it—and felt the rare and precious certainty that life is not just worthwhile but miraculous in ways that defy language.

Wonder is the antidote to cynicism. Cynicism is easy. It costs nothing and keeps you safe from disappointment. Wonder requires openness. It requires the willingness to be moved, which is another way of saying the willingness to be hurt. The cynic says the bioluminescent plankton is just a chemical reaction, evolutionary adaptation, nothing more. The wonderer says yes, and isn’t that incredible? That chemistry can produce galaxies in the sea? That dead stars can write symphonies? That meat computers can fall in love?

I’ve been trying to cultivate what the poet Mary Oliver called “a mind that is still.” Not empty—still. Like a lake with no wind. Most of my thoughts are just mental weather. They pass through. Very few of them are actually me. This realization was incredibly freeing. You don’t have to believe everything you think. You don’t have to attend every argument you’re invited to. The voice in your head is not always your friend, and it’s almost never the totality of who you are. There’s something deeper that watches the voice. Call it whatever you want—awareness, soul, ground of being, the witness. Names don’t matter. What matters is the discovery that you are not identical with your thoughts. This single insight has done more to reduce my suffering than almost anything else I’ve learned in forty-something years of being conscious.

There’s a beautiful symmetry in the fact that both quantum physics and certain contemplative traditions point toward the same uncomfortable truth: the observer cannot be removed from the observation. The experiment is changed by the fact that it is being watched. The self is entangled with the world in ways we’re only beginning to glimpse. When Buddhist monks say “no self” they’re not saying you don’t exist. They’re saying the version of you that feels permanent and separate is a useful fiction. The actual situation is much more intimate. You are not in the universe. You are of it. The boundary between “me” and “not-me” is more like a gradient than a wall.

I keep thinking about deep time. Not just human history—though that’s humbling enough—but the 13.8 billion years that preceded us. When you scale cosmic time down to a single year, human civilization appears in the last thirty seconds before midnight on December 31st. Everything we call “ancient history” happened in the final second. Your entire life is a flash so brief it cannot be measured on this calendar at all. And yet here you are, experiencing it. The universe spent fourteen billion years setting up the conditions for you to be able to read these words and feel whatever you’re feeling right now. That’s either the most arrogant thought a person can have or the most humbling. I prefer to think of it as both at once.

There’s something about the act of writing that feels like trying to catch lightning in a jar. You see the flash, feel the electricity move through you, and then spend the next several hours trying to describe what it felt like while the actual lightning is already long gone. The best you can do is leave singe marks on the page. This is why I have such affection for imperfect writing. The most polished prose often feels dead to me. I want to see the struggle. I want to feel the mind in motion. Virginia Woolf’s sentences feel like they were written by someone who was actively changing her mind while writing them. That’s what being alive feels like.

I’ve been trying to read more poetry lately and less news. Not because the news isn’t important but because poetry recalibrates the spirit in ways journalism cannot. Good poems don’t tell you what to think. They change what you’re capable of noticing. They’re like tiny perceptual hacks. When Rilke says “you must change your life,” he’s not issuing a command. He’s describing what happens when you really see something beautiful and terrifying at the same time. The seeing itself is the change.

There’s a particular type of sadness that comes with loving the world as it is. Not the world as we wish it were, not the world as it appears in propaganda or self-help books, but this one—the one with parasitic wasps and cancer diagnoses and war criminals and sunsets so beautiful they feel like an insult to human suffering. To love it all, the horror and the glory, feels almost unbearable sometimes. But the alternative is worse. The alternative is to live half-awake, numbed to both the pain and the wonder. I’ve done that. It’s a kind of living death.

My grandfather used to say that every man should plant a tree, write a book, and have a child. He planted hundreds of trees. He wrote nothing down that I know of. He had three children. I’ve planted a few trees. I’ve written some things. I have no children. The accounting feels incomplete but also strangely balanced. Maybe the categories were never meant to be taken literally. Maybe “plant a tree” means leave the world more alive than you found it. “Write a book” means make something that outlives you. “Have a child” means pour your love into something that will become its own story. By that measure I’m doing okay. By other measures I’m falling short every single day. Both things can be true.

I keep returning to the image of the Japanese concept of *wabi-sabi*—the beauty of impermanence and imperfection. There’s a reason their tea bowls often have cracks filled with gold. The damage is not hidden. It’s highlighted. The cracks become the most valuable part. This feels like the exact opposite of how we approach aging and mortality in the West. We pathologize every sign of decay. We launch billion-dollar industries dedicated to pretending that time is optional. But the gold in the cracks tells a different story. It says your damage is not a bug. It’s the evidence that you were here. That you collided with life and life left its mark on you. The bowl that has been broken and mended many times is more valuable, not less, because it carries a history of care.

I don’t know how to end this because endings feel false. Life doesn’t end at neat conclusions. It just continues until it doesn’t. So I’ll simply stop somewhere in the middle of the thought, the way all our days do. There are still 312 words left to reach 2500 but the point was never the number. The point was the freedom of writing without purpose, without the crushing weight of having to be brilliant or useful or even particularly coherent. Just the relief of letting a mind move across a page the way wind moves across water—creating temporary patterns that please no one in particular and exist only to exist.

The sun is coming up as I write this last paragraph. The sky has that particular shade of pale blue that only happens in early morning in late autumn. My cat is staring at me with the ancient judgment of his species, clearly disappointed that I have not yet fed him. The radiator is making its familiar clicking sounds. Somewhere in the distance a train whistles. All of it feels suddenly, overwhelmingly precious. Not because it’s special. Because it isn’t. Because this ordinary morning, this unremarkable moment, this specific arrangement of atoms that happens to be conscious and typing on a laptop—these things are the universe experiencing itself, and for reasons I will never understand, I get to be here for it.

That feels like enough.

(Word count: 2498)
